about: Lesson F11 (f11-air-climate-people). One tonne of coal, natural gas or oil burned: its heat and CO2 from the 2006 IPCC Guidelines' defaults; methane leaked before gas is burned, at a leak share the reader sets, as CO2e with the AR6 100-year GWP of fossil methane; air pollutants from EPA's AP-42 emission factors for large boilers, before and after the controls AP-42 describes; a spreading toy (illustrative) for where the particles go; EPA's 2025 benefit-per-ton values (estimates, 2019 dollars) for the health harm; then energy burden for Prairie City's household groups, read from prairie-city.json. The coal's sulfur and ash, the oil's sulfur, the controls chosen, the toy's spreading rule and the income slider are set for teaching and labelled so on the page.

fuelsAlso.name: Sub-bituminous coal
fuelsAlso.note: the coal most Plains plants burn; used in the Go deeper box only

ipcc2006.title: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, Volume 2 (Energy), Chapter 1 (Introduction)
ipcc2006.where: Table 1.2, p. 1.18 (default net calorific values, TJ/Gg = GJ per tonne): other bituminous coal 25.8, natural gas 48.0, gas/diesel oil 43.0, sub-bituminous coal 18.9; Table 1.4, pp. 1.23-1.24 (default CO2 emission factors, kg/TJ): 94,600, 56,100, 74,100 and 96,100; section 1.4.1.2, p. 1.16: net calorific values are about 5% below gross for coal and oil and about 10% below for most natural gas
ipcc2006.netNote: Net calorific values leave out the heat in the water vapour the fuel forms; the IPCC uses them.

carbon.note: Each tonne of carbon burned makes 44/12 = 3.67 t of CO2 (molar masses 44 and 12 g/mol).

gwpSource.title: IPCC Global Warming Potential Values, version 2.0 (adapted from the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report)
gwpSource.where: p. 2: 100-year GWP of fossil methane 29.8 (AR6), non-fossil 27.0; p. 1: the fossil value is for fugitive emissions from oil and gas systems and coal mining

studies.label: Alvarez et al. (2018), Science
studies.what: U.S. oil and gas supply chain, 2015: 13 ± 2 teragrams of methane a year, equivalent to 2.3% of gross U.S. gas production, about 60% above the EPA inventory's estimate (abstract)

studies.label: Sherwin et al. (2024), Nature
studies.what: six U.S. oil and gas regions measured from aircraft: total emissions from 0.75% to 9.63% of natural gas production, by region (abstract); 15 aerial campaigns from 2016 to 2021, the 0.75% in Pennsylvania (2021), the 9.63% in the New Mexico Permian (2018-2020) (p. 329 and Fig. 2); historical survey estimates, each for its campaign's period

methane.pureNote: The leaked gas is counted as pure methane; pipeline gas is mostly methane (AP-42 section 1.4: generally above 85 percent).

source.title: AP-42, Compilation of Air Pollutant Emission Factors, Volume I: Section 1.1 Bituminous and Subbituminous Coal Combustion (9/98); Section 1.3 Fuel Oil Combustion (5/10); Section 1.4 Natural Gas Combustion (revised 10/26); Appendix A (9/85, reformatted 1/95)
source.caveat: AP-42 factors are averages of tests: about half of real sources emit more and half less (Section 1.4's disclaimer).

coal.set: illustrative coal, within AP-42 Appendix A's ranges for bituminous coal (sulfur 0.6-5.4%, ash 4-20%)
coal.boiler: pulverized coal, dry bottom, wall-fired, bituminous (AP-42 Table 1.1-3)
coal.where: Table 1.1-3, p. 1.1-16 (SOx 38S lb/ton, NOx 22 lb/ton, 11 with low-NOx burners); Table 1.1-6, p. 1.1-26 (PM2.5 0.6A lb/ton uncontrolled, 0.024A with an ESP); Table 1.1-5, p. 1.1-24 (condensable PM 0.1S - 0.03 lb/MMBtu without FGD, 0.02 with FGD; 26 MMBtu/ton); Table 1.1-1, p. 1.1-13 (wet lime or limestone scrubbers, 80-95+%); lb/ton x 0.5 = kg per metric tonne (footnote a)

gas.boiler: large wall-fired boiler, over 100 MMBtu/hr (AP-42 Table 1.4-1)
gas.where: Table 1.4-1, p. 1.4-6 (NOx 190 lb per million scf uncontrolled post-NSPS, 140 with low-NOx burners); Table 1.4-2, p. 1.4-7 (PM total 7.6, all below 1 micrometre; SO2 0.6 at 2,000 grains of sulfur per million scf; fuel density 4.2 x 10^4 lb per million scf, footnote b)

oil.set: illustrative distillate oil, within AP-42 Appendix A's range (0.2-1.0%)
oil.boiler: No. 2 oil in a boiler over 100 MMBtu/hr (AP-42 Table 1.3-1)
oil.where: Table 1.3-1, pp. 1.3-11 and 1.3-12 (SO2 142S lb per 1,000 gal; NOx 24, 10 with low-NOx burners and flue gas recirculation); Table 1.3-6, p. 1.3-17 (filterable PM2.5 0.25 lb per 1,000 gal, industrial boilers); Table 1.3-2, p. 1.3-13 (condensable PM 1.3, all below 1 micrometre); Appendix A, p. A-7 (distillate oil 845 kg/m3)

controls.coal: a wet limestone scrubber (it catches 90% of the SO₂), low-NOx burners (a cooler flame forms less NOx) and an electrostatic precipitator (charged plates catch the particles)
controls.gas: low-NOx burners (a cooler flame forms less NOx)
controls.oil: low-NOx burners with flue gas recirculation (some exhaust is fed back to cool the flame); no scrubber

spread.set: illustrative toy, not a dispersion model: a year of winds from every direction spreads the particles in a widening ring; their concentration falls as 1/r while rain and the ground remove them over an illustrative reach L; people live evenly around the plant
spread.note: The toy starts 10 km out: closer to a tall stack the plume may not yet have reached the ground.

bpt.title: Technical Support Document: Estimating the Benefit per Ton of Reducing Directly-Emitted PM2.5, PM2.5 Precursors and Ozone Precursors from 21 Sectors
bpt.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Office of Air Quality Planning and Standards
bpt.where: Table 8, p. 22: 2025 values in 2019 dollars at a 2% discount rate, per short ton, PM2.5-related benefits (mortality and morbidity); electricity generating units: directly emitted PM2.5 $113,000, SO2 $57,000, NOx $7,710; residential wood stoves: directly emitted PM2.5 $479,000; p. 6: source-apportionment air quality modelling across the continental U.S., then health effects with BenMAP-CE
bpt.ozoneNote: PM2.5-related harm only; EPA lists ozone-related harm from summer NOx separately.

who.title: Ambient (outdoor) air pollution, fact sheet
who.where: 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019 from ambient air pollution, 89% of them in low- and middle-income countries; 99% of the world's people lived where WHO's air quality guideline levels were not met (2019)

aceee.title: How High Are Household Energy Burdens?
aceee.publisher: American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE)
aceee.where: a burden above 6% is called high and above 10% severe; with 2017 American Housing Survey data, 25% of U.S. households had a high burden and 13% a severe one

lead.title: Low-Income Energy Affordability Data (LEAD) Tool
lead.where: energy burden = home energy spending / income; 6% or more is called high; about 6% on average for low-income households (0-80% of area median income) and about 2% for others

facts.what: CO₂ from burning one tonne of bituminous coal, natural gas and diesel or heating oil (IPCC default values).
Tonnes of CO₂ that warm the climate as much over 100 years as one tonne of fossil methane (IPCC AR6, as compiled by the GHG Protocol).
Methane from the U.S. oil and gas supply chain in 2015, as a share of gross gas production: about 60% above the EPA inventory's estimate (study abstract).
EPA's 2025 estimate of the health harm avoided per short ton of SO₂ not emitted by U.S. power plants (2019 dollars): an estimate, not a price.
Premature deaths worldwide in 2019 from outdoor air pollution, 89% of them in low- and middle-income countries.
Energy burdens that ACEEE calls high and severe; DOE's LEAD tool calls 6% or more high. Conventions, not physical limits.
